[Messages]
[Presiding Judge]: Counsel:

Attached is the Court’s Revised Pretrial Scheduling Order. In light of the approaching trial date and the Court’s calendar, the deadlines set forth herein are firm. The parties are expected to cooperate in preparing a comprehensive joint pretrial statement, including a neutral statement of the case, a good-faith set of stipulated facts, and a focused list of contested issues. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in exclusion of evidence, monetary sanctions, or other appropriate relief.

IT IS SO ORDERED.

[Opposing Counsel]: Counsel,

We write in light of Judge Ramirez’s revised pretrial scheduling order entered this afternoon.

Attached please find our draft of the joint pretrial statement, including proposed stipulated facts and issues for trial. Given the compressed timeframe, we will need your revisions or confirmation no later than 5:00 p.m. two days from now so that we can finalize the submission and comply with the Court’s twelve-day deadline.

We have included as “undisputed” those facts that, in our view, are either already admitted in the pleadings or established by the current evidentiary record. We are also assuming that your client will withdraw the speculative consequential damages theories related to alleged downstream customer losses, which lack any admissible evidentiary support and, as you know, were the subject of the Court’s prior skepticism at the last status conference.

If your client is unwilling to narrow its theories accordingly or continues to contest facts that are plainly established, we will have no choice but to seek appropriate relief, including targeted motions in limine to exclude such evidence and an application for fees and costs associated with addressing positions we believe to be objectively unreasonable at this stage.

We remain available for a meet-and-confer tomorrow afternoon to discuss.

Best regards,

[Name]
[Law Firm]

[Client General Counsel]: Team,

Please see Judge Ramirez’s new order and the message we just received from [Opposing Counsel], both attached.

The deadlines are tight, and I’m concerned about the way they’ve tried to characterize the “undisputed” facts and to push us to drop the consequential damages component. At the same time, I don’t want us to pick unnecessary fights or invite sanctions, especially given the judge’s warnings in the order.

I’d like a structured view of our options here:

• How hard should we push back on their list of “undisputed” facts?
• Which of our damages theories are realistically worth preserving for trial in light of the evidentiary record and the judge’s prior comments?
• How should we respond to their implicit threat of motions in limine and fee applications, given the relatively short time before trial?

Please have the assistant sketch options and a draft response email to [Opposing Counsel] that outside counsel can mark up and send.

[Business Unit Executive]: Adding a quick business lens here:

The downstream customer piece is important to us in principle, but I recognize that if the evidence just isn’t there, we shouldn’t over-invest limited time and budget trying to save it at all costs. What I don’t want is for us to concede away leverage too quickly or agree to “facts” that could box us in at trial on the core liability issues.

I’d like to see options that preserve our ability to tell a credible story about what actually happened operationally, without picking every possible fight or creating more work than we can realistically handle on this timeline.

rounds.response: Options (brief): (A) Cooperate narrowly — accept truly admitted/pleaded facts to reduce fights and sanction risk but cede minor leverage; (B) Push selectively — agree to noncontroversial stipulations but dispute any “undisputed” items that would prejudice liability or credibility and preserve consequential-damages only where we can identify concrete evidentiary support (best balance of efficiency and preserving trial story); (C) Hard-line — refuse concessions and prepare preemptive motions/fee demands if Opposing persists (maximizes pressure but raises cost and risk of judge displeasure). Recommendation: adopt option B — produce a limited set of stipulated facts, push back on items that box us in, and preserve downstream damages only to the extent we can cite specific witnesses/documents/expert support now; propose a focused meet-and-confer to narrow issues and avoid unnecessary motions. Immediate tactical tasks: assemble a one-page evidentiary index for the downstream losses (witnesses, documents, expert plan), draft redlines to Opposing’s joint statement by the 5:00 p.m. deadline, and prepare a short warning that fee motions are unnecessary if they refuse reasonable narrowing. Draft email to Opposing Counsel for your mark-up: "Counsel — we received your draft and attach our redlines plus a short list of facts we accept as undisputed and those we dispute (with brief grounds). We are prepared to meet tomorrow at 2:00 p.m. (or 4:00 p.m. if needed) to finalize the joint pretrial statement; please identify any specific bases for anticipated motions in limine or fee applications by 5:00 p.m. two days from now so we can address them in the meet-and-confer. rounds.response:
Stipulation templates — Stipulate as‑is: "Undisputed: The parties agree that [concise factual statement supported by pleadings/record] (e.g., ‘On March 1, 2024, Company X executed Purchase Order Y’)." Stipulate with neutral wording: "Undisputed as rephrased: The parties agree that [neutral description of event] (e.g., ‘Between Jan–Mar 2023, the parties exchanged written communications regarding Product Z’), removing conclusory or argumentative framing." Dispute (do not stipulate): "Disputed: [concise description of the contested proposition]; proposed JPS language — 'Disputed: the parties disagree whether [specific legal/consequential assertion]; evidence and testimony will address causation/intent/effect.'"

Damages language (2–3 sentences): "Plaintiff preserves two specific downstream‑customer damage theories for trial: (1) direct lost orders and contract value from Customer A causally linked to the defendant’s actionable conduct, supported by contemporaneous emails, order histories, and witness testimony; and (2) Customer B’s contract termination and measured revenue loss, supported by the contract, termination notice, and documentary communications. We withdraw broader reputational, market‑ripple, and other generalized consequential damages theories that lack trial‑ready evidentiary support on this schedule, without prejudice to supplementing our position if timely, admissible evidence surfaces."

Meet‑and‑confer talking points (4–6, compressed): "We appreciate the background edits and want to agree noncontroversial, document‑based stipulations to narrow the trial; we will insist that any stipulation avoid legal conclusions and preserve disputed issues on causation, intent, and remedy; we will provide a one‑page evidentiary index for Customer A and B by tomorrow to support keeping those damages theories; we are prepared to negotiate neutral wording for borderline facts but will not abandon core factual or causation contentions without seeing Opposing’s evidentiary basis; we prefer resolving non‑material disputes by agreement to avoid motions, but will seek judicial resolution for any issue that meaningfully impairs our liability or damages case.
